newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: Police prepare for day protests in Papua New Guinea.
newsitem.headline: Police prepare for day protests in Papua New Guinea.

text.p: Armed police set up roadblocks around Papua New Guinea's Parliament House on Tuesday as pressure grew for the resignation of Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan over his government's hiring of foreign mercenaries.

Police, some carrying M16 rifles and shotguns, stopped cars and questioned people ahead of an expected protest, set to coincide with an afternoon sitting of parliament where the opposition will call on the prime minister to step down.
Chan is facing a motion to force him to resign over a $36 million contract with the British firm Sandline International for mercenaries to crush a rebellion on Bougainville island.
Thousands of demonstrators were expected to gather outside parliament and demand his resignation and there was concern about whether the army would take part in a planned march.
Local media said on Tuesday that police had given the army permission to march as long as troops were unarmed.
Banks, schools and shops were all ordered to close for fear of a repeat of violence which followed a demonstration last week outside the army barracks.
The opposition will put a motion calling on Chan to resign when parliament begins at 2.00 p.m. (0400 GMT).
Chan, who has so far resisted all calls for his resignation, also faces a petition from the army calling on him to quit.
Support for Chan was further eroded on Monday when five ministers, including three from his own party, either resigned or promised to resign. There was speculation more would follow.

The crisis, the worst in Papua New Guinea's 22 years of independence, began a week ago when army chief Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok turned against Chan and demanded that he terminate the mercenary contract and quit.
Chan sacked the general and tried to ride out the storm but Singirok, popular with his troops, remained in effective control of the army as violent protests increased pressure on Chan.
Opposition politicians and resigning ministers appeared on local radio on Tuesday morning urging calm, but repeating their calls for Chan to step down.
Opposition leader Roy Yaki said the country had been forced into a "serious crisis".
"We as members of parliament have been very clearly put to a special task to ensure that within our abilities that we save this nation from total chaos and bloodshed," he said.
He called for a caretaker government to be appointed until national elections, due in June.

"The question is not a question of alternative government," Yaki said. "The question is whether it is in the interest of Papua New Guinea that he (Chan) should continue as prime minister of this country."
Michael Somare, the country's first prime mininster and regarded as the father of the nation, appealed for calm and for people to obey the law.
"I am appealing for Papua New Guinea's people to stay cool, calm and allow the normal democratic process to take its course," Somare said.
Former agriculture minister David Mai, who resigned on Monday, said on radio that the merceneary deal had never been discussed in cabinet.
"Cabinet never endorsed the Sandline deal. Therefore in my view it is unconstitutional," he said.
Mai said he expected more cabinet ministers to quit and to call on Chan, his deputy Chris Halveita and defence minister Mathias Ijape, to step down.
He also said he supported Singarok's actions and did not beleive they were treasonous.
"That was a responsible act on the part of a responsible citizen of this country," Mai said.
The week-long crisis has preoccupied Papua New Guinea's Pacific neighbours.
Australia, its former colonial power, has had troops on standby to help around 10,000 Australian nationals who live in the country if the situation deteriorates.
